claims.claim: London's 'Knowledge' taxi-licensing test requires learning around 25,000 streets plus thousands of landmarks and points of interest.
claims.episode_span: drivers must master “The Knowledge,” memorizing roughly 25,000 streets and thousands of points of interest
claims.source_title: The Knowledge | London Electric Vehicle Company
claims.supporting_quote: It involves learning 320 routes, around 25,000 streets and 20,000 points of interest and has even been found to improve people’s memory.

claims.claim: MRI research found London taxi drivers have a larger posterior hippocampus than the general public.
claims.episode_span: MRI scans published in 2000 showed that these drivers developed a measurably larger posterior hippocampus
claims.supporting_quote: A study showed that the posterior part of the hippocampus is larger in these drivers than in the general public, and that a positive correlation exists between the length of time served as a driver and the increase in the volume of this part.

claims.claim: Posterior hippocampal volume in London taxi drivers correlates positively with time spent driving the city.
claims.episode_span: the volume of that region correlated directly with years spent driving the city
claims.supporting_quote: a positive correlation exists between the length of time served as a driver and the increase in the volume of this part

claims.claim: Eleanor Maguire's taxi-driver study, 'Navigation-related structural change in the hippocampi of taxi drivers', was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2000.
claims.episode_span: MRI scans published in 2000 showed that these drivers developed a measurably larger posterior hippocampus, the brain region most involved in spatial representation
claims.supporting_quote: Maguire, E. A.; Gadian, D. G.; Johnsrude, I. S.; Good, C. D.; Ashburner, J.; Frackowiak, R. S. J.; Frith, C. D. (2000). "Navigation-related structural change in the hippocampi of taxi drivers" . Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . 97 (8): 4398– 4403.

claims.claim: Eleanor Maguire is best known for her long-running series of studies on London taxi drivers documenting hippocampal structural change.
claims.episode_span: Neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire’s long-running studies of London taxi drivers provided the clearest before-and-after contrast
claims.supporting_quote: Perhaps the most famous of these is her series of studies on London taxi drivers

claims.claim: GPS Selective Availability, which degraded the civilian signal, was switched off in May 2000.
claims.episode_span: continuous positioning signals could guide vehicles and aircraft with meter-level accuracy once selective availability was switched off in May 2000
claims.supporting_quote: On May 2, 2000 "Selective Availability" was discontinued as a result of the 1996 executive order, allowing civilian users to receive a non-degraded signal globally.

claims.claim: fMRI research (Javadi et al., Nature Communications 2017) found hippocampal activity tracked the street network only during active navigation, not when participants were simply told which turns to take.
claims.episode_span: Several studies now report reduced activity in the same hippocampal areas during wayfinding tasks when turn-by-turn instructions are available
claims.source_title: Hippocampal and prefrontal processing of network topology to simulate the future | Nature Communications
claims.supporting_quote: Furthermore, hippocampal activity was significantly more positively correlated with the change in degree centrality during Navigation routes than Control routes

claims.claim: Experts publicly warned that automatic wayfinding erodes natural navigation abilities (e.g., a 2016 Nature comment by Roger McKinlay).
claims.episode_span: A few cognitive scientists noted that constant reliance might affect memory
claims.source_title: Technology: Use or lose our navigation skills | Nature
claims.supporting_quote: Automatic wayfinding is eroding natural abilities, warns Roger McKinlay.
